title: Thin Equity: How a Finished Building Is Still Lost
summary: A building can be finished on time and to specification and the developer can still lose it, because equity that is thin relative to the project's uncertainty cannot absorb an overrun. Leverage magnifies the demand for fresh cash, not merely the loss.
body:
Mr Shabazz, some projects fail because the building breaks; others fail although the building is perfect, because the money behind it could not absorb a surprise. Equity is thin when it is small relative to the project's uncertainty, not relative to its cost.

In plain English

Equity is the owner's own money in the project, the part not borrowed. It is the first money spent and the last money repaid, so it absorbs every overrun until it is gone. If the overrun is larger than the equity cushion, the owner must find new cash quickly, on the lender's timetable, or lose control of the project. This lesson is a composite post-mortem of how that happens, not an account of any real developer.

Thin compared with what

A lender sizes his loan to protect his own downside; he is not sizing your equity to protect your survival. Those are different questions. Equity of 30 percent of cost might be comfortable on a simple building on proven ground and dangerously thin on a complex one on soft ground with a long approval path. The judgement is the owner's, and it should start from a list of what could go wrong and how much each item could cost.

Funded and unfunded contingency

A contingency is money set aside for the unforeseen. A funded contingency is real money, inside the budget and the financing, available when needed. An unfunded contingency is a sentence in a document saying overruns will be covered, with no source of cash behind it. Only the first is a cushion.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical project of 100 units of total cost, financed at an illustrative 70 percent loan to cost. These numbers are illustrative, not market practice.

  1. The loan is 70 and the owner's equity is 30.
  2. Costs overrun by 15 percent. Total cost becomes 115.
  3. The loan was sized at signing and does not grow: the lender still advances 70.
  4. Equity must cover 115 minus 70, which is 45. The owner's cash requirement goes from 30 to 45.
  5. A 15 percent cost overrun is a 50 percent increase in the equity call: 15 more on a base of 30.
  6. At 80 percent loan to cost, equity would be 20 and the same overrun would demand 35, a 75 percent increase. Leverage amplifies the demand for fresh cash, not merely the loss.
  7. Now add time. If the overrun also brings four months of delay, interest and preliminaries continue during those months, so the true overrun is larger than the construction cost line suggests.

How it unfolds

The pattern is usually slow and then sudden. The contingency is consumed early, often in the ground. The lender's monitor reports that the remaining budget no longer covers completion. Draws stop until the owner funds the gap. The owner tries to raise money while the project is visibly in trouble, which is the most expensive time to raise it. New equity arrives on hard terms, or the lender enforces. The building is later finished and is a good building; it simply belongs to someone else.

What Design-Build does and does not fix

A lump-sum Design-Build price is a real defence against this failure, perhaps the strongest argument for the method, because it moves the risk of many overruns to the contractor. But it is only as good as the scope definition behind it: a thin brief creates scope disputes that land back on the owner. And it does not remove owner-side risks such as approvals, ground beyond any baseline, owner changes, interest on delay or a weak leasing market.

Sizing equity honestly

Start from the project's real uncertainties: ground, approvals, design maturity, price escalation, schedule and market. For each, estimate a plausible bad case. The equity plus funded contingency should survive a realistic combination of them, not just the lender's minimum. Then add standby liquidity: committed cash or credit outside the project that you can draw without asking anyone's permission.

The early-warning signs

Thin equity rarely announces itself. Watch for four signs: contingency being drawn faster than the work is progressing, so that half the contingency is gone at a quarter of the programme; change orders pending approval that, if approved, would exceed what remains; the lender's monitor qualifying his monthly report; and the owner starting to delay payments to consultants to protect cash. Any one of them is a reason to model the equity call again that week, not at the next quarterly review. The earlier the owner raises new money, the more of the project he keeps.

Keep the model simple enough to update in ten minutes: total forecast cost, committed loan, equity spent, equity still to come, and standby liquidity. If forecast cost minus loan exceeds equity plus standby liquidity, the problem already exists; it has simply not reached the bank yet.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing equity to the lender's minimum and treating the minimum as safe. The lender's minimum protects the lender. Your margin is a separate number, and on uncertain ground it is larger.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts a contingency that has no cash behind it, or counts the same reserve twice, once in the budget and once as his personal safety margin. Ask of every cushion: where is the money, and who must agree before I can use it?

How you will use it

Before committing, run the overrun arithmetic at 10, 15 and 20 percent and see what each does to your equity call. List the project's real uncertainties and size funded contingency to them. Arrange standby liquidity in advance. Treat the lender's equity requirement as a floor, not a target. Professional sign-off required: an accountant and a development finance adviser; counsel for any equity documents.
checklist: Run the equity call at 10, 15 and 20 percent overruns before committing.
Size equity to the project's uncertainty, not to the lender's minimum.
Count only funded contingency as a cushion.
Include interest and preliminaries during delay in any overrun scenario.
Arrange committed standby liquidity before you need it.
Remember a lump sum protects you only as far as its scope definition.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A project costs 50 million at 75 percent loan to cost. Costs overrun by 12 percent. What happens to the equity requirement, in money and in percentage?
selftest.a: The loan is 37.5 million and equity 12.5 million. Cost rises to 56 million; the loan stays at 37.5 million, so equity must cover 18.5 million. That is 6 million more, a 48 percent increase in the equity call from a 12 percent cost overrun.

apply: Write a one-page list of five uncertainties on a hypothetical project with a plausible bad-case cost for each, and compare the total with a 5 percent contingency.
sources: Composite example; no real developer described. Leverage arithmetic is standard finance. Loan to cost and contingency levels are commercial practice, not standards. All figures hypothetical.

title: The Wrong Debt: Guarantees, Reserves, Covenants and Cross-Default
summary: Loan terms can turn a manageable problem into a lost project: recourse, the completion guarantee, an interest reserve sized to the plan, covenants that act as tripwires, and cross-default. These terms often cost more than the interest rate and deserve the most reading.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the interest rate is the most negotiated number in a construction loan and rarely the most important. The guarantee, the reserves, the covenants and cross-default decide what happens when things go wrong, and that is when debt actually hurts.

In plain English

A loan agreement is a set of promises with consequences. When the project is going well, most of those promises do nothing. When it goes badly, they decide whether the owner has time to fix the problem or loses control. This lesson covers the terms that matter most in that moment. All of them are commercial terms, negotiated between parties; their effect and enforceability depend on the documents and the jurisdiction.

Recourse

A non-recourse loan is repaid only from the project; if it fails, the lender takes the project and generally cannot pursue the owner's other assets, subject to carve-outs for things like fraud or misapplied funds. A recourse loan allows the lender to pursue the borrower or guarantor beyond the project. Many construction loans are partly or fully recourse during construction. Know which you are signing and which assets stand behind it.

The completion guarantee

A completion guarantee is a promise, usually by the sponsor personally or by a parent company, to complete the building at the guarantor's own cost if the project's funds run short. In many forms it is unlimited in amount. It is often the least-read document a first-time developer signs and the one with the largest personal consequence. A lump-sum construction contract does not remove it: lenders commonly require it whatever the price structure, because they want the sponsor's money behind completion, not only the contractor's promise.

The interest reserve

An interest reserve is part of the loan set aside to pay interest during construction, because the building earns no income yet. It is sized to the planned programme. If the programme slips, interest continues and the reserve runs out, often in the same months that an overrun is already squeezing the budget. Delay and overrun tend to arrive together.

Covenants

Covenants are conditions the borrower must keep: completion by a date, a minimum level of pre-leasing, a maximum loan to value, cost to complete within the remaining budget. Breaching one is usually an event of default, even if every payment has been made. Treat each covenant as a tripwire and ask what the cure period is and what the lender may do if it is not cured.

Cross-default

A cross-default clause makes a default on one loan a default on another. For a developer with several assets, it is how three good projects follow one bad one: a covenant breach on the troubled building triggers default on the healthy ones, which may then be called or repriced.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical construction loan of 7,000,000 with an interest reserve of 600,000, sized for an 18-month programme at an average interest cost of about 33,000 a month.

  1. At month 15 the programme is four months late. The reserve has about 3 months of interest left, roughly 100,000, but 7 more months are now needed.
  2. Seven months at about 50,000 a month, higher now because the loan is nearly fully drawn, is 350,000. The shortfall is about 250,000.
  3. The completion covenant date is month 20; completion is now forecast at month 22. A covenant breach is coming.
  4. The lender's cost-to-complete test also fails, because the same delay raised preliminaries. Draws stop until the owner funds the gap.
  5. The owner has a second building financed by the same lender with a cross-default clause. The default on the first now threatens the second.
  6. The completion guarantee requires the sponsor to fund completion from personal resources. The total call is the interest shortfall, the preliminaries overrun and any construction overrun, all at once.

Reading the documents in the right order

Read a loan package in the order that the bad case would unfold, not the order it is bound. Start with the events of default and their cure periods, then the covenants that trigger them, then the remedies the lender gains, then the guarantees that follow, and only then the pricing. Ask counsel one question for each: in our realistic bad case, does this clause apply, when, and what does it cost us? A loan that looks cheap in the pricing schedule can be the most expensive one in the bad case.

Ask for a guarantee that shrinks as risk falls. A completion guarantee that falls away at practical completion, or is capped and reduced as the frame tops out and the envelope closes, matches the guarantor's exposure to the lender's actual risk.

And keep the guarantee inside your personal balance sheet thinking. A sponsor with three projects and three completion guarantees has, in the bad case, three calls on the same personal assets.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing an unlimited completion guarantee and a cross-default clause without modelling what both would demand in a realistic bad case.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner spends his negotiating effort on a quarter of a point of interest and accepts standard guarantee and covenant terms. Negotiate cure periods, the size of the interest reserve, the covenant dates with realistic margin, carve-outs from cross-default, and, where possible, a cap or burn-off on the guarantee once milestones are met.

How you will use it

Before signing, list every covenant with its test, its date and its cure period. Model the interest reserve at plus four and plus eight months. Read the completion guarantee and the cross-default clause with counsel and model their effect in a bad case. Ask for cure periods and milestone-based reductions. Professional sign-off required: finance counsel and an independent development finance adviser.
checklist: Know whether the loan is recourse and which of your assets stand behind it.
Read the completion guarantee with counsel and model its call in a bad case.
Model the interest reserve at four and eight months of delay.
List every covenant with its test, date and cure period.
Find every cross-default clause linking this loan to your other assets.
Negotiate cure periods, realistic covenant dates and guarantee caps or burn-offs.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A lender offers a lower interest rate in exchange for an unlimited completion guarantee and cross-default to your other two projects. How do you weigh it?
selftest.a: Model the bad case: a delay that exhausts the interest reserve and an overrun that fails the cost-to-complete test. The guarantee would call on your personal resources and cross-default could put the other two projects at risk. A small rate saving rarely justifies that exposure; negotiate a capped or milestone-limited guarantee and no cross-default, even at a slightly higher rate.

apply: Draw up a one-page covenant table for a hypothetical loan: covenant, test, date, cure period, and what happens if it is not cured.
sources: Recourse, completion guarantees, interest reserves, covenants and cross-default are standard construction finance terms; their content and enforceability depend on the documents and jurisdiction, and they are commercial terms, not law. Example hypothetical and composite.

title: Foundation Risk Through a Credit Officer's Eyes
summary: The foundation phase is the lender's worst position: highest uncertainty and almost no recoverable value. Lenders respond with equity-first sequencing, contingency sized to the uncertainty you did not buy down, and an in-balance covenant, and each of these can be negotiated.
body:
Mr Shabazz, to a credit officer, money spent below ground is money he cannot get back if the project stops. That is why foundation risk shapes your equity, your contingency and your covenants, and why buying down ground uncertainty pays twice.

In plain English

If a project stops halfway up the frame, a lender can still sell a partly built building. If it stops in the foundations, there is very little to sell: a hole, some concrete and a lot of uncertainty about what it would cost to finish. So the lender is most exposed exactly when the ground is least known. Everything he asks for in this phase follows from that.

The lender's three responses

These are commercial practices, not standards, and vary by lender and market.

First, equity-first sequencing: the owner's equity is spent before any loan money is advanced, so ground surprises are paid from the owner's money.

Second, contingency sized to uncertainty: a hard-cost contingency, often discussed in a range around five percent of hard cost for ordinary work and more where uncertainty is higher. Ask the lender; never assume. The less ground uncertainty you have bought down, the more he wants.

Third, the in-balance covenant: the remaining undrawn loan plus remaining equity must always cover the remaining cost to complete. If an overrun breaks that balance, draws stop until the owner deposits the difference.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical hard cost of 100 units, of which substructure is 10, with a hard-cost contingency of 4. Illustrative figures only.

  1. The investigation was thin. During excavation, soft clay is found thicker than expected under one zone, and the engineer requires piles there.
  2. Substructure rises by 60 percent, from 10 to 16: an increase of 6.
  3. The contingency of 4 is gone, and 2 more is owed, before the ground slab is cast.
  4. The in-balance test fails by 2. Draws stop until the owner funds it.
  5. Add time: redesign, piling mobilisation and testing add eight weeks. At a combined weekly time cost of 60,000, using Week Two's illustrative rate, that is about 480,000 of interest and preliminaries on top.
  6. Now the counterfactual. A supplementary investigation costing perhaps 0.2 units would have found the clay, the piles would have been in the base budget, the contingency would have been intact, and the lender might have accepted a lower contingency because the biggest uncertainty was measured.

The negotiation thread

Trade evidence for contingency: offer a thorough investigation, a baseline in the construction contract and fixed piling rates, and ask for a lower contingency because the uncertainty it covers has been reduced. Ask for a ground-specific allowance that steps down once foundations are certified complete, so cushion that is no longer needed is released to the rest of the job. Accept the in-balance covenant, because every lender needs it, but negotiate its cure: how long you have to fund a shortfall and in what form, such as cash, a letter of credit or a guarantee. Keep a second lender in conversation; your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, your BATNA, is what gives your requests weight.

The second-order effect

A ground surprise rarely stays in the ground. It consumes contingency that was meant for the whole job, so a later, unrelated overrun, in finishes or services, now arrives with no cushion left. Ask how the contingency is drawn and who approves it, and track what remains against the work still to be done, not against the original total.

Recoverable value

Why is foundation work worth so little to a lender? Because value in an unfinished building depends on someone being willing to finish it. A buyer taking over a stalled site pays for what is useful to him: completed frame, envelope, services. Foundations he cannot see, cannot verify without testing, and may have to redesign around are discounted heavily. So a lender's loss in a stopped project is roughly the money advanced minus what a buyer will pay for the work in place, and below ground that difference is close to the full amount. Understanding that one point explains every request he makes in this phase.

It also explains why lenders like testing records. Pile load tests, special inspection reports and certified as-built records turn hidden work into evidence a buyer can rely on, which raises its recoverable value.

Keep those records organised from the first pile, because the lender's monitor, a future buyer and a future insurer will all ask for the same documents.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a thin investigation paired with a minimum contingency, in a loan with a strict in-balance covenant and a short cure period. That combination turns one soft zone of clay into a stopped project.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees the investigation fee as a cost to minimise. To the lender, it is the cheapest risk reduction available, and it can reduce the equity and contingency he requires by far more than it costs.

How you will use it

Present the geotechnical evidence to lenders as part of the credit case. Ask for a ground allowance that steps down after foundation certification. Negotiate the in-balance cure period and form. Track contingency remaining against work remaining every month, and report it to the lender before he asks, because a borrower who reports his own problems early is treated very differently from one whose problems are found by the monitor. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, development finance adviser, and finance counsel.
checklist: Expect equity to be spent first and ground surprises to land on it.
Ask each lender how he sizes contingency; never assume a figure.
Present the geotechnical investigation as evidence to justify a lower contingency.
Ask for a ground allowance that steps down after foundations are certified.
Negotiate the in-balance covenant's cure period and acceptable forms of cure.
Track contingency remaining against work remaining every month.
Keep a second lender in conversation as your alternative.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your lender proposes a 7 percent hard-cost contingency, higher than you expected, citing ground risk. You hold a thorough investigation and fixed piling rates. What do you propose?
selftest.a: Offer the investigation, a ground baseline and the fixed piling rates as evidence that the main uncertainty is measured, and ask for a lower general contingency plus a specific ground allowance that steps down once the foundations are certified. Accept the in-balance covenant but negotiate a reasonable cure period and form. Keep a second lender's terms in hand.

apply: Using hypothetical numbers, show what a 50 percent rise in substructure cost does to a contingency of 4 percent of hard cost when substructure is 12 percent of hard cost.
sources: Equity-first sequencing, contingency practice and in-balance covenants are commercial lending practice that varies by lender and market, not standards. Contingency percentages quoted are illustrative. Example hypothetical.

title: When the Ground Changes the Budget Inside a Joint Venture
summary: In a joint venture, a foundation change is three events at once: a decision needing the investor's approval, a capital call, and a lender in-balance event, each on its own clock. The joint venture agreement decides who decides, who pays, what happens to a partner who cannot pay, and how deadlock is broken.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when partners share a project, a cost surprise is not only a money problem; it is a governance problem with three clocks running at once. The dilution from failing to fund is usually small; the loss of control is what destroys a developer.

In plain English

A joint venture brings together a developer, who manages the project and usually contributes a minority of the equity, and an investor, who contributes most of the money. Their agreement says how decisions are made and how money is called. When foundations cost more than planned, the developer needs the investor's approval to change the budget, both partners must fund their share of the extra cost, and the lender's in-balance covenant is already counting down. If the clocks do not line up, the project can be in default before the partners have finished talking.

The four questions a joint venture agreement answers

Who decides: the managing member handles day-to-day decisions, but listed major decisions, often including budget increases above a threshold and changes to the foundation design, need the investor's consent. Who pays: capital calls require each partner to fund its percentage within a stated period. What happens if someone does not pay: remedies include straight dilution, penalty dilution, the funding partner treating its extra contribution as a member loan at a high interest rate, and, in some agreements, removal of the managing member for cause. How deadlock is broken: by escalation, mediation, a buy-sell mechanism or an expert. These are commercial terms; wording varies widely.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical venture with total equity of 40: the developer contributes 4, which is 10 percent, and the investor 36. A piled foundation adds an overrun of 8 that must be funded with equity.

  1. Pro rata, the developer owes 0.8 and the investor 7.2.
  2. The developer cannot fund; the investor funds all 8.
  3. Straight dilution: the developer's share becomes 4 divided by 48, about 8.3 percent, down from 10.
  4. Penalty dilution at 1.5 times: the investor's extra 0.8 counts as 1.2, so total contributed counts as 48.4, and the developer's share becomes 4 divided by 48.4, about 8.26 percent.
  5. The dilution is small either way. The real threat is elsewhere: many agreements let the investor remove the developer as manager for a funding failure or a default, and removal often forfeits the developer's promote, the share of profit above his equity percentage that was the main reason to do the deal.

The sequencing trap

Suppose, hypothetically, the investor has 15 business days to approve a budget change, then the partners have 30 days to fund the call, while the lender's in-balance cure period is 30 days from notice. Approval plus funding can take about 51 calendar days; the lender's clock expires at 30. The loan can be in default before the investor is even obliged to answer, and a loan default may itself be grounds to remove the manager. Align the clocks at signing.

What to negotiate at signing

A ground allowance pre-approved in the budget, so a foundation change within it is not a major decision. Deemed approval on time-critical decisions if the investor does not respond within a short period. A protective capital call whose timing matches the lender's cure period. A cure right for the developer before removal, with a reasonable period. Protection of promote already earned. And, as the developer's alternative, committed standby liquidity so that funding the small share is never in doubt. All periods, percentages and multiples are commercial practice, not standards.

The investor's view

The investor is not the villain here. He is protecting a much larger share of money against a manager whose fees continue whether or not the project succeeds, which is a classic incentive and agency problem. Terms that give the developer speed in an emergency are easier to win when they come with transparent reporting and an early warning duty.

Reporting as a governance tool

Much of the friction in a venture comes from surprise. An investor who learns of a foundation problem at the same moment as the capital call will approve slowly, ask for an independent review and question the manager. One who has seen monthly reports showing contingency remaining against work remaining, and an early-warning note the week the soft clay was found, is far more likely to approve within days. Build an early-warning obligation into the agreement on your own initiative: a short written notice to the investor within a few days of any event likely to require a major decision or a capital call. It costs the developer little and buys speed when speed matters most.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is three clocks that do not line up: approval, funding and lender cure. When they are misaligned, the venture defaults while everyone is still acting in good faith.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner focuses on the dilution arithmetic, which is small, and ignores removal and promote forfeiture, which are not. He also assumes his partner will approve quickly because it is obviously necessary.

How you will use it

Map every clock in the joint venture agreement and the loan on one timeline. Negotiate a ground allowance, deemed approval, aligned call periods, a cure right before removal and protection of earned promote. Hold standby liquidity. Report early and in writing whenever a major decision or capital call is likely. Professional sign-off required: joint venture counsel and finance counsel, working from the same timeline, because a joint venture agreement drafted without sight of the loan agreement is how the clocks come to disagree.
checklist: Map the approval, capital call and lender cure clocks on one timeline.
Pre-approve a ground allowance so a foundation change is not a major decision.
Negotiate deemed approval for time-critical decisions.
Align the protective capital call period with the lender's cure period.
Secure a cure right before removal as manager.
Protect promote already earned.
Hold committed standby liquidity to fund your share.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your joint venture gives the investor 20 business days to approve a budget change and 30 days to fund, and your loan gives 30 days to cure an in-balance shortfall. What is wrong, and what do you change?
selftest.a: Approval plus funding can take about two months, while the lender's cure expires in 30 days, so the loan can default before the partner must respond. Negotiate a pre-approved ground allowance, deemed approval on time-critical decisions, and a protective call that matches the lender's cure period, and hold standby liquidity for your share.

apply: For a hypothetical venture where you hold 15 percent of equity of 20, compute your share after straight dilution if your partner alone funds an overrun of 4.
sources: Joint venture governance, capital calls, dilution, removal and promote are commercial terms that vary widely by agreement; periods and multiples quoted are illustrative, not standards. Example hypothetical and composite.

title: Week Five Review: Equity, Debt, Covenants and Partners
summary: Six scenario questions on leverage, contingency, loan terms, the in-balance covenant and joint venture governance. The week's thread is that a good building can still be lost through the money behind it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week was about losing a project that was built correctly. Work each question aloud before reading the answer, and keep the arithmetic in round numbers.

Question 1. A project costs 100 at 70 percent loan to cost. Costs overrun by 20 percent. What happens to the equity call?

Answer. Equity starts at 30. Cost becomes 120; the loan stays at 70; equity must cover 50. That is 20 more on a base of 30, a 67 percent increase in the equity call from a 20 percent overrun. Leverage amplifies the demand for fresh cash.

Question 2. Your budget shows a contingency of 5 percent, but you have no cash or committed facility behind it. Is it a cushion?

Answer. No. An unfunded contingency is a sentence in a document. A cushion is money inside the budget and the financing, available without anyone's permission. Fund it or remove it from your margin of safety.

Question 3. The interest reserve covers an 18-month programme. The job is now four months late. Which other terms are likely to bite at the same time?

Answer. The completion covenant date, the lender's cost-to-complete or in-balance test because preliminaries rose with the delay, possibly a pre-leasing covenant, and the completion guarantee once project funds fall short. If the loan has cross-default with other loans, those assets are exposed too. Delay and overrun arrive together, which is why the reserve should be modelled at plus four and plus eight months before signing.

Question 4. Hard cost is 100 with substructure 12 and contingency 5. Substructure rises by half. What happens?

Answer. Substructure becomes 18, an increase of 6. The contingency of 5 is gone and 1 more is owed before the ground slab. The in-balance test fails and draws stop until the owner funds it, and the delay that came with the change adds interest and preliminaries on top. Negotiate in advance a ground allowance that steps down after foundations are certified, and a workable cure period.

Question 5. In a joint venture you hold 4 of 40 in equity. An overrun of 8 is called and you cannot fund your 0.8, so your partner funds all of it. What happens to your share, and is that the real threat?

Answer. Straight dilution takes you to 4 divided by 48, about 8.3 percent from 10; a 1.5 times penalty takes you to about 8.26 percent. The dilution is small. The real threat is removal as manager and forfeiture of your promote, which many agreements allow after a funding failure. Hold standby liquidity so you can always fund your share.

Question 6. Your joint venture allows 15 business days to approve a budget change and 30 days to fund; the loan allows 30 days to cure an in-balance shortfall. What is the trap?

Answer. Approval plus funding can run to about 51 calendar days, while the lender's cure expires at 30. The loan can be in default before your partner must answer, and a loan default may itself trigger your removal. Align the clocks at signing: a pre-approved ground allowance, deemed approval, and a protective call that matches the cure period.

Recap

Before the recap, notice that none of the six answers depended on an interest rate. Each turned on a term: a ratio, a reserve, a covenant, a cure period, a removal clause. That is where construction finance is won and lost, and it is where an owner's reading time is best spent.

Equity is thin when it is small relative to uncertainty, not to cost. The lender sizes the loan to protect himself; the owner sizes equity to survive. A cost overrun raises the equity call by a larger percentage, and the more leverage, the larger. Only funded contingency is a cushion. A lump-sum contract helps, but only as far as its scope definition.

The wrong debt is the debt whose terms turn a problem into a loss: recourse, an unlimited completion guarantee, an interest reserve sized to the plan, covenants that act as tripwires, and cross-default that spreads one failure across a portfolio. Negotiate the structure, not only the rate.

Below ground the lender has the most uncertainty and the least recoverable value. He responds with equity first, contingency sized to uncertainty, and an in-balance covenant. Buy down the uncertainty with investigation and trade the evidence for a lower contingency and a ground allowance that steps down.

In a joint venture a foundation change is an approval, a capital call and a lender event, each on its own clock. Dilution is small; removal and promote forfeiture are not. Align the clocks and hold standby liquidity.

The thread: a finished, well-built building can still be lost through the money behind it, and the terms that decide that are fixed before the first draw. Professional sign-off required: development finance adviser, accountant, finance counsel and joint venture counsel.

One test ties the week together. For any financing structure, write down a realistic bad case, a soft-ground surprise and four months of delay, and walk it through every document in order: the construction contract, the loan agreement, the guarantee, the joint venture agreement. If you cannot say on what day each clause bites and who must act, you do not yet understand the deal you are about to sign.

Next week returns to site, to the structures nobody sees in the finished building: formwork, falsework and props, which carry the permanent building before it can carry itself.
checklist: Run equity-call arithmetic at several overrun levels.
Count only funded contingency.
Model the interest reserve against delay.
Read the guarantee, covenants and cross-default before the rate.
Negotiate in-balance cure periods and ground allowances.
Align joint venture clocks with lender clocks.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Name the two terms in this week's lessons that most often decide whether an owner keeps control of a troubled project.
selftest.a: The in-balance covenant with its cure period, which decides how quickly draws stop and how long you have to fund a shortfall, and, in a joint venture, the removal-for-cause provision, which can take away management and promote after a funding failure. Completion guarantees and cross-default decide how far the damage spreads.

apply: Draw a single timeline for a hypothetical project showing an overrun discovery, the joint venture approval and funding periods, and the lender's cure period, and mark where they conflict.
sources: Review of Lessons 21 to 24; see those lessons for sources. All ratios, periods and percentages are commercial practice and illustrative. Examples hypothetical and composite.
